segments.text: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me, Norman Swan. Today, for all you back pain sufferers, another pain reliever bites the dust. So what's left, you might ask?
But there is a pain reliever which might be an effective treatment for depression, although there could be a catch, isn't there always?
An astounding one in ten people will have a seizure during their lives. Some of them will have epilepsy, but the definitions are changing.
and influenza.
The flu season is almost upon us.
We're being exhorted to be immunized,
but how reliable is this year's flu vaccine?
And should we be worried about the deaths
occurring in southern China at the moment from bird flu?
They do have the World Health Organization worried
because it's not just China.
There's a chicken cull on in Japan at the moment.
Just in case it isn't safe to go out,
we thought we'd preview the flu season.
And with me here in Melbourne to do that
is Dr. Alan Hansen,
who chairs the Influenza Specialist Group.
Welcome to the Health Report, Alan.
Good evening, Norman.
So what's in this year's vaccine?
There are four strains in this year's vaccine.
We put in two influenza A viruses,
which are representative of two quite distinct subtypes of influenza A.
And there are two influenza B viruses.
They're not as different one from the other as the influenza A viruses,
but they represent two lines of influenza B which have diverged since the 1980s.
And is there much difference?
I mean, would you know whether you're hit with an A or a B?
Or is B nastier than A or what?
It depends who you are, I think.
What we do tend to find is that children are more affected by the influenza B viruses than adults.
And adults, particularly older adults, are more severely affected by one of the influenza A viruses, the H3N2.
But that pandemic virus, which struck us in 2009, 2010.
H5N1.
No, H1N1.
H1N1, sorry.
It's still around, and it's still affecting younger adults to a much greater degree than the other A virus does.
And is that covered by the current set of vaccines?
Yes, it certainly is.
In fact, the strain that covers that has just been updated this year.
So how do you know which to put in?
It's a long process.
So it's better than roulette?
No, not quite.
But it's really based on surveillance, worldwide surveillance through about 120 laboratories contributing to WHO's programme.
And then twice a year now we have an evaluation of all the information that's available.
So these tend to be the viruses that are circulating in the northern hemisphere that we expect to come down south?
It's a combination because we also see viruses circulating through the tropical areas out of those seasons.
So if you go back to last year, which was a trivalent, I think it was only three last year?
No, last year, I think for the first time, we did have a quadrivalent vaccine.
The year before, we had trivalent vaccine.
So how many were missed by the vaccine?
How effective was the vaccine relative to what actually hit Australia last year?
It was very close to the circulating strains.
What we don't see, though, is 100% protection, unfortunately.
That's a function of influenza vaccines.
the nature of the vaccines, but also the nature of the people who receive them.
Older people in particular, we try to vaccinate. And as you get older, your immune system tends to
wane. So we can't protect people as we might have been able to when they were younger.
And that's one of the reasons why we do try to vaccinate people more widely,
people who are in contact with high risk people and people in the older age.
So who should be immunized?
Well, certainly anybody over the age of 65 should be immunised.
Anybody with a pre-existing risk condition, such as heart or lung disease, kidney disease,
diabetes, things of that nature, and pregnant women who are particularly susceptible to
the ill effects of influenza.
But pregnant women and their GPs often think it's risky to have an immunisation in pregnancy.
I think we're winning them round.
They have thought that vaccination was not good.
But GPs tend and obstetricians tend not to want to undertake any treatment that's not absolutely necessary.
But I think they're now seeing, particularly in result of the 2009 pandemic, where we saw huge impact in pregnant women.
We're getting the message through now that it is both safe and effective.
So talking about effective, there's been a controversy about that.
Some people say it doesn't save the number of hospital bed days that it's purported to, or indeed the number of lives.
Is it effective?
It is effective, but it's not 100%.
In fact, the effectiveness may be closer to 50% or 60%.
And this is one of the reasons why the more people we vaccinate, the greater the effect is going to be.
Because you lower the amount of circulating flu.
That's right.
So tell us about the stuff, what's going on in southern China.
I mean, this really toxic virus, it's 40% mortality rate, which sounds terrifying.
Are we at risk?
What's going on?
Is there another pandemic sitting there in the background?
We never know when a pandemic is going to arise.
I mean, we've been watching the H5 virus, which has circulated through, more recently
through the Middle East, but previously through Southeast Asia.
That was the H5 virus.
This one's called H7N9.
Now, this one, the new one is H79.
It's only been circulating for about the last five years in China.
In a way, it's more dangerous than the H5 virus.
Because you can't pick it up in the chickens because they don't get sick.
That's right.
And the H5 virus, you do see high death rates in the birds.
And we're still seeing that in parts of the world with the H5 virus.
So what's not happening to make it a pandemic?
Is this human-to-human transmission?
Yes, we don't get any ongoing human-to-human transmission.
There might have been a rare case of human-to-human transmission,
but the virus has not yet acquired that ability.
This has been the great fear for the last 15 years with the H5 virus
is that it will acquire that ability to spread,
and it really caused a lot of activity in terms of pandemic preparedness planning.
Now, the H7 has come along,
and it looks a little more likely to be able to spread from person to person,
but it's still quite a way of being able to do that.
Any coverage from the current vaccines?
No, none at all.
So it may be safe to go out.
Who knows?
Alan Hampson, thanks for joining us.
My pleasure, Norman.
Alan Hampson from the Influenza Specialist Group.
And you're listening to The Health Report here on RN,
ABC News Radio and CBC Radio across Canada.
I'm Norman Swan.
Most of us will have an episode of back pain sometime in our lives
and sometimes the pain will radiate down one leg
and be called sciatica.
and in a proportion of people that pain can last for weeks or months
and can involve weakness and numbness.
Over the last couple of years, the health report has run stories
on how paracetamol is pretty rubbish for back pain
as are the so-called anti-inflammatories like ibuprofen.
These studies have emanated from the George Institute in Sydney
and now a group of Australian and overseas researchers have dug deeper
and looked at a medication that's supposed to target nerve pain
to see whether that works
and they published their findings in the current edition of the New England Journal of Medicine.
The drug is called pregabalin.
The brand name is Lyrica and Lyrica prescriptions have been booming.
But does it work for sciatica?
Christine Lynn of the George Institute is in our Sydney studio.
Welcome to the Health Report.
Thank you for having me, Norman.
So why would you think pregabalin would work,
pregabalin I should say would work, Lyrica would work in back pain?
Well, we have some evidence that pregabalin works for other types of nerve pain
and as you've already mentioned that sciatica which is often related to the nerve roots of
coming out of our lower spine is considered a type of nerve pain so we thought that pregabalum
may be also effective for sciatica. And to what extent have prescriptions been booming?
Well just to give you an example in Australia pregabalum the medicine came onto the market
was approved by the Australian government for use of nerve pain in 2013.
And in 2014, 1.4 million scripts were written.
In the next year, that number went up to 2.4 million,
and that was 30% more than the government originally predicted.
And worldwide, pregabalin is actually the number one selling drug for nerve pain.
Gosh. And presumably it's not cheap.
Well on the prescription
It does cost people money
And also it has side effects
So that's why we designed this study
To find out whether it's truly effective or not
For this patient population
So tell us about this study
So in this study we recruited more than 200 people
Who had at least
Who had sciatica of at least moderate
If not severe intensity
These people had pain that was bad enough for them to present to a GP for care.
And when they entered the study, they were randomly given either the active or the placebo medicine.
And the patients were kept blinded as to which medicine they received in order to keep the study as unbiased as possible.
And presumably the doctors were blinded too as well.
Yeah, the doctors and also the other study personnel were also blinded.
and the patients were...
And so this was both acute sciatica and chronic.
It had lasted for a while.
That's right.
So we recruited patients who had had at least one week of pain
up to one year of pain.
Yeah.
And these patients were put on the medicine for about eight weeks,
up to eight weeks,
and the dose was adjusted for them according to their progress by their doctor.
And what were you looking for as outcomes?
Our most important outcome was leg pain because that's the most significant pain in a patient
when they experience sciatica.
And we collected the outcome mainly at eight weeks.
That was the main time point that we were interested in.
But we also followed the patients up over one year.
And in addition to leg pain, we collected a range of other relevant clinical outcomes,
such as if they had any back pain or if they were functioning okay.
So what did you find?
What we found was at eight weeks, there was absolutely no difference between the patients
who took the active medicine compared to the patients who took the placebo medicine in
terms of how bad their leg pain was.
We also saw the same thing at one year.
And this was also the same at eight weeks and one year for all the other outcomes that
we measured.
What about side effects?
Because it's not side effect free.
That's right.
And that's the concern.
And what we found was the people who took the active medicine had nearly twice as many side effects.
Such as?
Such as dizziness.
Dizziness was actually the main side effect.
And sedation, you can get sedation with Lyrica too, can't you?
Yeah, yeah.
I think so.
Dizziness and drowsiness.
So the drug needs to be carefully used in people operating heavy machinery or in elderly people.
So does it work in other nerve pain?
I mean, why didn't it work in back pain if the nerves are involved in the sciatica?
Well, there's some evidence that it works out for other types of back pain.
Back pain or nerve pain?
Sorry, other types of nerve pain.
But one of the main reasons why we think it hasn't worked for sciatica
is that pain mechanism is a lot more complex than we thought.
So even though sciatica is considered a type of nerve pain,
there may be other mechanisms at play, including psychosocial factors.
So explain more.
In other words, but that's true of all pain.
I mean, all pain is affected by psychosocial factors.
If you're feeling stressed, if you're depressed, you know, the pain can make you depressed.
I mean, it's a very complex thing, pain, and back pain is not alone in that.
You know, chronic headaches, chronic arm pain, they all have psychosocial factors.
Pain is never simple.
Yeah, exactly.
And so I think we're only beginning to understand pain and there's a lot more to be studied.
But this also shows that we really need to test each drug specifically for each patient condition.
So a drug that can work for another pain condition may not be able to work for back pain or sciatica.
Well, we're kind of running out here.
We've found that paracetamol is not much cop.
Paracetamol plus codeine is not much cop.
Ibuprofen, the anti-inflammatories, aren't much cop.
You've got an epidemic of opiate prescribing in the United States
for things like chronic pack pain and sciatica
without much evidence that it does much more than just kill you.
I mean, what's left?
Well, that's the problem.
I think the picture is quite depressing in terms of the treatment options.
I think the most important thing is when people have sciatica,
they're reassured that the pain will get better.
and other than that unfortunately we don't know
we don't have a good answer for what medicines people can take
in order to help them get better quicker.
So have we shown that physio works, chiropractic,
manipulation of the back?
Yeah, so for sciatica there's also unfortunately no convincing evidence
that other forms of, that physiotherapy works
or other forms of physical therapies work.
and surgery is dubious.
Although with sciatica,
there's probably better evidence
than just low back pain.
Yeah, that's right.
So for surgery,
there is evidence that surgery works
in selected patients over the short term.
But after one year,
the results are the same
in people who haven't had surgery.
So it is really up to the individual's condition.
What a cheery conversation, Christine.
Yeah.
We look forward to your next trial,
which hopefully we'll find something positive.
Luke, but seriously though, thank you very much.
Good trial and in a great journal.
Thanks very much.
Thanks, Norman.
Associate Professor Christine Lynn
of the George Institute for Global Health
at the University in Sydney, I should say.
Now, another painkiller is ketamine.
It's used by ambulance officers in cases of trauma
because it doesn't lower blood pressure
if you've had a head injury or you're bleeding.
And it's also used in anesthesia.
Ketamine's also, unfortunately, become a drug of abuse.
But it's also known to help relieve depression.
The trouble is that it has to be given by injection and it could be dangerous if taken repeatedly.
But that hasn't stopped doctors around the world, including Australia, from prescribing it.
Which is why the Black Dog Institute in Sydney is carrying out a trial of ketamine in people with depression.
And one of the investigators is with us now in our Sydney studio.
It's Colleen Liu, who's Professor of Psychiatry and Director of the Sydney Neurostimulation Centre.
Welcome to the Health Report.
Hi Norman.
So what is the evidence that ketamine helps depression?
Look, there's very good evidence, Norman,
but many from studies that have examined the effects of a single treatment.
So we started with this ourselves as well about five years ago in Sydney
at the University of New South Wales.
And I must say that I was astounded by the results I saw,
that people who were highly treatment resistant, severely depressed,
who had failed 10 or more medications,
could become completely well and free of depression
within 24 hours of a single dose of ketamine.
Given by intravenous infusion?
Look, in that case, we actually gave it by, so we actually tried a few things, intravenous infusion.
We also tried injecting it into the muscle or just under the skin.
And we've also tried actually sniffing the drug through the nose.
But whichever way you give it, it still seems to work quite well.
How long for?
Well, see, that's...
Actually, before we come to how long for, I mean, in that sort of situation,
that's when electroconvulsive therapy is used, ECT,
to try and get a quick response,
particularly if people are suicidal
and you really need to dig them out of their deep depression.
Has anybody compared it to ECT?
Yes, indeed.
There's a small study from overseas that has done that.
And remarkably, it found that ketamine worked as well as ECT,
but even more quickly.
I think that's preliminary and that still needs to be replicated.
And there are now studies around the world doing that.
But you're right.
it's that population that we're treating, people with fairly severe treatment-resistant depression.
And how long, going back to that question actually before I'm so rudely interrupted you,
how long does it last for when you give one dose?
Well, see, that's the catch, Norman. And for a lot of people, it doesn't last. So that you do
tend to relapse back into your depressed state after a few days. Curiously, for some people,
and we wrote up a case of someone we treated where we gave her a very small dose, and she was actually
well for five months. And this is someone who had failed to gain multiple medications. So that's
one of the things that we're still trying to understand in research, which people are going
to have what kind of response to ketamine. So tell me about the study that, tell me about the
study you're doing. Okay. So one of the strategies that clinics in Australia and around the world
have started to use because a single dose works so well is, well, why not then give repeated doses?
And so they're doing exactly that.
But the problem with just giving repeated doses is we don't actually know how well does it work.
So, for example, you know, will you keep having a good response or will you actually start having a kind of a tolerance where after a while the drug doesn't work as well?
And how many doses should you give and how do you determine the dosing?
And also, is it safe?
You know, when you give a single treatment that, yes, in the short term, you have passing side effects over the next hour or so.
But when you give repeated treatments, then there are different implications for safety.
So it's liver and bladder side effects, isn't it?
So there are some quite potentially serious side effects.
And we know of this mainly from knowledge in recreational drug users.
And this is one of the problems.
It hasn't been studied adequately under controlled conditions.
But you can get quite serious bladder problems where you actually get an inflammation or even a kind of a necrosis, a dying off of the lining of your bladder.
This is not a trivial problem because then you can get scar tissue.
It could make you depressed as well.
That's right.
But, you know, you can then lead on to some permanent bladder problems.
So this is something that it's very important for people to be aware of.
And again, you see, the studies looking at a single dose don't have this problem
because it's mainly an issue when you use it repeatedly.
I'm told anecdotally that there's an epidemic, for example,
of bladder problems in places like Hong Kong
where there's a high rate of ketamine abuse.
Are a lot of doctors using ketamine in Australia at the moment,
even though it's off-label, they're not supposed to?
Yeah, and look, off-label doesn't mean necessarily not supposed to,
just that it's not one of the indications that's published for the use of ketamine.
So there's an increasing interest in using ketamine,
and colleagues do consult me about it.
The problem, I think, Norman, is that we haven't yet worked out
what is the treatment protocol for using ketamine to treat depression,
and does it work with repeated dosing and is it safe
or how do you need to use it for repeated dosing for efficacy and safety?
And just to give you an example,
there are cautionary tales published in the literature case reports
and also clinicians who have come to me
where they've had someone who's very treatment resistant,
they've given them ketamine, it works wonderfully the first time,
then it wears off so they think, oh, well, let's give them a second dose,
it doesn't work quite as well.
And they've fallen into the trap of giving people higher and higher doses
and more and more frequently.
Then after a few weeks, a person is...
Sort of chasing it down a hall, basically.
Exactly.
And after a few weeks,
a person is right back where they started,
as depressed as when they started.
But now they're receiving a substantial dose of ketamine every day.
And then they're worried about stopping
because a person might then rapidly deteriorate
and become even worse.
So you've started with someone who was stably depressed
and then got caught in that trap
where you're giving them ketamine
and they're just as bad as they were.
But if you stop, they're likely to become even worse.
Now, it works in a different way.
We haven't got much time left,
but it works in a different way from the usual antidepressant drugs.
Can it be given with them and does it make them more effective?
Yes.
So in our trial that we're running, funded by the NHMRC,
we just have people usually on their stable doses of antidepressant medications
and we give ketamine on top of that because there's no reason for stopping them.
But you're right that ketamine works on a different neurotransmitter system,
different chemicals in the brain, which is why it's a fascinating drug
and which probably explains why it works so differently.
You don't normally expect to see a rapid response
a day after starting an antidepressant medication.
So briefly then, if somebody's got severe treatment-resistant depression
and your doctor wants to give you a single dose of ketamine,
that's probably evidence-based,
but you're potentially getting to tiger country with repeated doses
and hold off until you know what your results of your trial is.
Exactly.
So our trial is looking at the efficacy and safety of repeated dosing.
It looks at a four-week dosing protocol.
It's a double-blind trial, but also with an open-label treatment
so that you can go on to have active treatment.
And I'm really interested, you know, beyond that,
in getting funding to look at what a six-month treatment protocol should look like.
Because I think that's the ultimate aim.
How can we make this a clinically useful treatment?
Well, we'll book a slot for you to get the results on the health report.
Thanks for joining us, Christine.
Thank you.
Colleen, I should say.
Professor Colleen Liu, who is Professor of Psychiatry at the University of New South Wales and the Black Dog Institute.
One in 200 Australian children live with epilepsy.
Four people in a hundred will be diagnosed with epilepsy during their lives.
And no doubt when you hear the word epilepsy, you think of a grand mal seizure where someone falls to the ground, going stiff and blue and then jerking violently.
But epilepsy is often far more subtle and complicated and not always easy to diagnose and understand,
which makes it even more astounding that two-thirds of people
labelled as having epilepsy are not referred to an epilepsy specialist.
All these are among the reasons that the way the different types of epilepsy
should be classified has had its first revision in 30 years.
One of the experts behind this is Professor Ingrid Sheffern,
who's a paediatric neurologist and epidemiologist at the University of Melbourne
and co-winner of the Prime Minister's Science Prize in 2014
for her work on epilepsy.
Welcome, Ingrid.
Thank you very much, Norman.
So, suffice it to say, this is complicated.
We don't have three years.
We have about seven minutes.
Just tell us why the reclassification and what's the net effect of it?
Well, it was a desperate need to bring it up to date.
Science has moved on.
Epilepsy has moved on since 1989.
And we needed to bring in the new concepts to how we look at patients, how we make diagnoses,
how we look for causes, very importantly.
And that, of course, influences treatment.
So it was very timely, but it is complex.
And as Einstein said, it should be as simple as possible, but no simpler.

And that is something we really struggled with, was trying to get it so that it was using words that mean what they say and would be something that patients could use, doctors could use and everyone around them.
And you say in your paper that the science is not yet up to a proper classification.
that you can't classify like cancer or diabetes,
so you just take a practical approach, an operational approach,
rather than a science-based approach.
Yeah, but there's a lot more science informing it now than 30 years ago,
and that, of course, will change dramatically in the next 10, 20 years.
So take us through some of the big changes.
Well, I think the big changes are the framework for how we approach
when you see somebody with their first seizure or, in fact, epilepsy if it's uncontrolled.
And first you want to know the type of seizure they have.
So we have a whole new framework of new terms for seizures, which are meant to be more transparent.
And then we take them up to trying to diagnose their epilepsy type and ideally their epilepsy syndrome.
You can't always make a syndrome diagnosis.
By syndrome, you mean what?
By syndrome, I mean types of seizures that might occur together.
So people often have three or four different types of seizures and you need to know what goes with what.
And then the EEG or the brainwave tracing and what that shows.
and then maybe the MRI as well.
And you put that all together to make an epilepsy syndrome diagnosis.
And a good example is childhood absence epilepsy, where a child stops and stares.
So take us through the classical types of epileptic seizures or fits
and what they look like and how it changes.
Okay.
Well, the seizure types don't change, but the words have improved.
So you have two big groups where they begin in one part of the brain,
which were called partial and now called focal.
And in focal seizures, which are 60% of all epilepsy,
so the biggest group, you can be with it,
which we call an aware seizure now.
So you know you're having it.
So a focal aware seizure, exactly.
Which when I was a medical student, that told you it wasn't epilepsy at all,
but now we know it is.
Exactly.
And now impaired awareness.
So instead of what was complex partial,
and that didn't, complex doesn't mean not knowing where you are,
but impaired awareness does.
So now it's focal impaired awareness seizure.
That diagnosis is critical.
If you have it, you can't drive.
So it's a really important one for our society.
So it has an impact.
And so these focal epilepsies, that can be an unusual behaviour.
You stand up and walk to the end of the room and you don't know where you are when you come round.
So you can just be a bit confused off the air, we often say.
You might look to one side.
You might go pale.
You might do nothing.
It can be really boring to look at.
So in the old days, this is what was called Petimol, is it?
Well, that's the problem with the French.
Everyone loves the petit male and the grand male.
But in fact, they meant a host of different seizure types.
So they went out in 1981.
All right, sure to how up to date I am.
And we've now been working on these other ones.
So there's a focal group.
And then the other big group are the generalized groups,
which start in both sides of the brain at once and involve the old grand male
means tonic-clonic, where you go stiff, tonic, and clonic, jerking.
So stiffen and jerking, and you fall to the ground with loss of consciousness.
And the other main well-known ones are absence.
So you stop and stare, often just for five seconds,
and then you're back with it.
And the third big one is the myoclonic seizure, where you jerk.
So then go down a level.
So that's like, if you like, exactly what's happening to you
and describing it for what it is.
The causes, I mean, the reason you and Sam Berkovic got the science prize,
the PM science prize, was for your work on the genetics of this.
Exactly.
So the causes are now up front and centre.
From the moment you see somebody with a seizure,
you have to ask yourself, what's the cause?
And when we started in what we're doing,
there were no genes known for epilepsy.
We found the first one in 1995 with John Mulley from Adelaide.
And that really has made...
Genetics has since come to the fore
with the new next-generation sequencing techniques,
the new gene-finding science.
And we now have about 400 genes known for epilepsy.
So there are many.
Mostly in childhood epilepsy or first seizure in adults?
Because the first seizure in adults, the alarm bells ring.
Does this person have a malignant tumour, for example?
What's going on here?
So more in childhood and adolescent onset,
but some adults can have genetic forms as well.
And they may have malformations.
And we know that there are subtle malformations of the brain
that cause focal epilepsies.
But there are a whole host of other causes that we now think about.
including structural changes and metabolic changes.
Where can people go to find out more?
Well, the International League Against Epilepsy
is the international body that defines epilepsy.
And this is like the DSM-5, if you like,
which is for psychiatry, but the equivalent for epilepsy.
And so you can look at their website to get more information.
And get a referral to an epileptologist
rather than sticking with the doctor who doesn't necessarily...
Oh, I think lots of paediatricians and neurologists
are very capable with epilepsy, so they'd be perfectly good too.
Ingrid Sheffer, thanks for joining us.
Thank you.
Professor Ingrid Sheffer is a paediatric neurologist
and epileptologist at the University of Melbourne.
I'm Norman Swan.
This has been The Health Report
and I hope you can join me next week.
